utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in the court this morning. Mr. Registrar, can you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, and good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-83-T, the Prosecutor versus Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could we have the appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, and everyone. Laurie Sartorio and Kyle Wood for the Prosecution. We're assisted by our case manager, Fraser McIlwraith.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to my learned friends from the OTP, to everyone in and around the courtroom. I am Vasvija Vidovic, with Mr. Nicholas Robson, representing Mr. Delic, with our legal assistant, Lana Deljkic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Vidovic. May the witness please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Sir, you may now be seated and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And good morning to you. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Madam Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This witness's statement has been admitted pursuant to Rule 92 bis, and therefore we'll just be proceeding right into cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, sorry for the interruption. Just for the record, the statement of the witness, which has been -- which was admitted on the 5th of December, will be Exhibit number 970.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Exhibit number 970, witness statement. Thank you very much, Mr. Registrar. Yes, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Omerasevic. My name is Nicholas Robson, and I'll be asking you some questions today on behalf of General Rasim Delic. Just to explain to you, you have prepared two statements to the Office of the Prosecutor. The first was dated the 24th of October, 2006, and the second was dated the 8th of May, 2007. Those two -- those two statements have been admitted into evidence with the Trial Chamber, and the Trial Chamber have read those statements. They will therefore be aware of what you say in those statements. The reason for you coming today is so that we today can clarify some of the points that you mention in the statements. If at any time you do not understand any of my questions, please let me know, and I'll try to rephrase them. Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED OMERASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Omerasevic, in 1995 you were the deputy commander of the 5th Battalion of the 328th Brigade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED OMERASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: The commander of the 5th Battalion was Ahmet Sehic; is that so?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED OMERASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And am I right in saying that at the time of the combat operations in September 1995, the headquarters of the 5th Battalion was in the village of Marici?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED OMERASEVIC
utterances.text: Marici.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So the headquarters was located in that village.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED OMERASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And is it also correct that your unit, the 5th Battalion, also had a rear command post in the village of Borovnica?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED OMERASEVIC
utterances.text: It wasn't in the village of Borovnica. It was between the Sehici and Borovnica villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. I now want to turn to your first statement, given in October 2006. And in that statement, at paragraph 39, you mentioned the El Mujahedin Detachment and you explain how, as far as you can remember, that unit was involved in operations at Podsjelovo. Now, would you agree with me that apart from the El Mujahedin Detachment, there were other Mujahedin groups operating in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED OMERASEVIC
utterances.text: Officially I don't know about the El Mujahid Unit. I do mention it in my statements sometimes as "El Mujahid." This is what the others referred to it. I don't know if there was some other such group. There were all sorts of stories, but officially I don't know. On the other hand, I never managed to find out where the El Mujahid Unit was located, at which level of command in the hierarchy of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina they belonged, and the only thing I am sure of is that the brigade command did not have any authority or jurisdiction over them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: You say that -- during September 1995, is it right that you were primarily located at the command post at Marici?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED OMERASEVIC
utterances.text: It was a provisional forward command post of a unit of the 5th Battalion. In order to avoid confusion, it was a forward command post that was set up before the preparations for the action itself. We received an order that Ahmet Sehic conveyed to me orally to place it along the line of defence, this forward command post, and to place two-thirds of the soldiers. That was the first order.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So that is a place where you would spend some of your time in September 1995.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED OMERASEVIC
utterances.text: I think 10, 12, 13 days I was there at that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And is it right that you would also spend some of your time in September 1995 in Borovnica?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED OMERASEVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't in Borovnica during those few days, since when I would be leaving the forward command post, I would turn left towards my house before that, because the next village to the left of Sehici is my village, where I live, Lijevca. And I didn't really pass that way in the last month or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Was your village, Lijevca, close to Borovnica?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED OMERASEVIC
utterances.text: It's about 20 minutes, not taking the road that the cars go but if you take a -- a path, pedestrian path.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Were you aware -- were there -- to your knowledge, were there any Mujahedin fighters based in Borovnica during September 1995?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED OMERASEVIC
utterances.text: Officially I don't know, and I didn't see any, but I did have one piece of information. Since we from the Marici area waited for ten days, we didn't know how the action was proceeding, Sehic and I decided by ourselves, without the knowledge of the brigade command, to take the unit that was at the line of defence when the order was issued for the other soldiers to come to the line of defence, to send them home to change clothes, bathe, take some more clothes, because it came on its shift. So when that group of soldiers returned, they were saying that there was a group of Arabs which, according to what they saw - because they were only at home for a couple of hours, between 5.00 and 7.00, that's how long it took them to get ready, because they walked on foot over the hill - so the group they noticed was different from the groups that they would see before then. More or less all of them were smoking, and there was a small shop there, and they would come to that shop and ask to -- to see if there was any beer to buy, which was a bit different from all the Arabs that they had met to the -- to date. And then in that story, before the beginning of the Vozuca action, people were guessing that this was a group of Kurds. I don't know how true this is. All I know is what I know based on the stories told by 10 or 15 soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you've mentioned the events in September 1995. In your first statement, you explain how on the 10th or 11th of September, around 4.00 or 5.00 in the morning, shooting started towards the area of Paljenik. You explain at paragraph 66 how later that day you received information about what was going on and you heard that the BiH army was attacking at the area of Vozuca. Do you remember saying that in your statement?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED OMERASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: In your statement, then you continue to explain how at around 10.00 in the evening of that day you were ordered to take the forest behind the village of Kesten, and you made a request to your commander, Ahmet Sehic, and asked if you could take the forest in the morning. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED OMERASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: You then explain how the next morning at 5.00 you went down towards Kesten village together with a unit of the 5th Battalion, and that unit was led by Ismet Sogolj [Realtime transcript read in error "Sokolj"]. You then explain that you established a new front line -- you established a new front line and then you and Ismet Sogolj decided to return to the visit -- to the village of Kesten. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED OMERASEVIC
utterances.text: We didn't decide to return to the village of Kesten. It was a couple of hundred metres away. But, however, Ismet, in agreement with me, was going back to the village of Kesten, where he had a certain number of company -- the company that had remained, and I was going back to Jasicka Kosa, where my forward command post was at that time and where I had a telephone connection, a field telephone connection.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that your forward command post at Jasicka Kosa was located on top of a hill that overlooked Kesten village?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED OMERASEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you could see maybe a half or a little bit more than a half of the village from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So as I understand it, you went from Kesten village back to your forward command post. And while you were at the post, you looked down and you could see that there was a group coming from the forest towards Kesten village. And at that point, on seeing the group, you decided to go down to Kesten to see what was going on. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED OMERASEVIC
utterances.text: First I heard shooting in the woods, and then after 10 or 15 minutes I could see people coming out of the woods going towards the houses in the village along the macadam road. Since I didn't have any communications with my soldiers or Ismet Sogolj, as the company commander, I tried to use a field telephone, because the communications man was next to me, to see if I could get in touch with Ahmet Sehic in Marici to see if he knew what was going on, and he said that he didn't know. And then after that, I had no other choice. I made the decision, left the communications man in the trench, and then I went to the village of Kesten myself to see what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And is it correct that as you walked down to Kesten, on your way to Kesten village you met some of your soldiers who were -- who were escorting some Serb women and you told those soldiers to take the women to the 5th Battalion's forward command post at Marici?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED OMERASEVIC
utterances.text: It's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: In your statement, you go on to explain what you saw in Kesten village. You say that you saw Ismet Sogolj arguing with Arabs outside a hall. You also explain how you saw four or five Arabs in the room inside the hall and maybe 40 to 50 Serb prisoners of war. Now, the Trial Chamber have read your account of what you saw in and around the hall, but what I would like to ask you specifically about is the following: In both statements, you refer to the men who took the Serb prisoners of war as "Arabs." Am I right in saying that those men that you called Arabs, in terms of their appearance, they had no insignia or markings that could identify them as belonging to a particular group?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED OMERASEVIC
utterances.text: You are correct, because they didn't have any insignia for me to be able to know which unit they belonged to. I must be sincere, though. The day before, there was a decision made about the insignia worn by the soldiers of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but since we had already started moving, I didn't know what the other units of the armija were wearing, what their insignia was, other than the units of the 5th Battalion. So sometime in the afternoon on that day, from a messenger from the commander of the brigade, I received a new code word for the 328th Brigade, a new password.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: But just to be absolutely clear, in terms of the appearance of these Arabs that you saw in and around the hall, there was nothing about their clothing from which you could conclude that they were members of the El Mujahedin Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED OMERASEVIC
utterances.text: No, they were not wearing all the same clothing. Some had camouflage uniforms with darker colours. Some had such uniforms of lighter colours. The clothes they were wearing were not uniform, and I didn't see any unit insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, you describe how the Serb prisoners of war were led towards Krcevine. Can you confirm the Krcevine village is along the road to the north of Kesten?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED OMERASEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'll try to orient myself. It is to the north of Kesten, I think, and it's a good 2 kilometres through wooded terrain, and then you get to a little hill where the village is. Maybe it's some 7 to 8 to 10 kilometres. That's where it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: In your statement, you explain that you travelled to the forward command post at Marici, taking the two boys, or young men, with you. Did you go there in a vehicle?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED OMERASEVIC
utterances.text: We took a -- a van, a TAM van, T-A-M van.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: You explain in your statement that as you passed Krcevine village, you saw the prisoners of war there. Is it right to say that that was the last time you saw those prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED OMERASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: How long did it take you to travel from Kesten village to Marici approximately?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED OMERASEVIC
utterances.text: Maybe 15 or 20 minutes. It's a bad macadam road, and it's not more than 7 or 8 kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And by the time you arrived in Marici village, is it correct that you found out that the Serb women had already been taken by what you describe in your statement as "another group of Arabs"?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED OMERASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, because I found one of the two soldiers there with whom the women were sent to the forward command post of the company, and he told me, when we came down from the forest road, to the road, there was 100 metres to the forward command post. Then a group of Arabs came along and they took those women from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: In your statement, you used the word -- you use the expression "another group." Is it your understanding that the Arabs that took the three women were members of a different group from the Arabs that took the Serb prisoners of war in Kesten village, or are you unable to say?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED OMERASEVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't say. It was a different group in relation to the group that happened to be in Kesten at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, you said that the last time you saw the Serb prisoners of war was in Krcevine village. It follows from that that after you arrived in Marici, at no point did you see the captured Serbs traveling through Marici village at any stage. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED OMERASEVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't, because it was already getting dark. If we're talking about the time when I came from Sehici with those two young men that we had brought out, when we arrived at Marici, I returned to Jasicka Kosa again and I spent the night there. But in the morning, 4.00 or 5.00 in the morning, an order came that we would need to switch our unit to the Cevaljusa region, a unit of the 5th Battalion, which is what we did. And then between 9.00 and 10.00, we took the whole 5th Battalion unit in that -- to that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I'm moving to a slightly different issue. As I understand your evidence, the Serb prisoners of war were taken by the Arabs on the second day of the September operation. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED OMERASEVIC
utterances.text: Well, all of that was happening on the second day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So if the operation started on the 10th of September, it would follow from that that the Serb prisoners of war were taken on the 11th of September. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED OMERASEVIC
utterances.text: Captured on the 11th of September, then, but then as for Krcevine, I don't know whether they were taken away on that day or some other day. I don't know. Anyway, the last time I saw them there was in the early evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. I now want to ask you about some reports that were sent around that period of time. It's correct, isn't it, that the superior unit to the 5th Battalion was the 328th Brigade, which was commanded by Fuad Zilkic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED OMERASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that Major Zilkic was obliged to send regular daily combat reports about his subordinate units, which included the 5th Battalion, to his superior unit?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED OMERASEVIC
utterances.text: Either I did not understand you properly or you misspoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I will repeat myself. Would you agree with me that Major Zilkic was obliged to send regular daily combat reports to his superior unit and the subject matter of those reports were his subordinate units, which included the 5th Battalion?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED OMERASEVIC
utterances.text: Now you expressed yourself in a better way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And the answer to my question? Would you agree with -- that what I put to you is correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED OMERASEVIC
utterances.text: Well, on the next day -- I mean, if all of this started on the 10th, then on the morning of the 12th, around 4.00 in the morning, I got this oral order. I would call it an "order," because it came from a higher instance to a lower instance. So I was orally ordered by Sehic to transfer the unit to the area of Cevaljici [as interpreted]. And on the same evening --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: We may be at cross-purposes. I'll start again. I'm speaking in general terms and I'm asking you this question in your capacity as a deputy commander of the 5th Battalion. Would you agree with me that commanders of units were obliged to send regular daily combat reports to their superior units?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED OMERASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that in general terms, Fuad Zilkic, as the commander of the 328th Brigade, was obliged to send reports each day about his subordinate units?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED OMERASEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what the agreement was, in terms of the chain of command, the brigade, the division, the corps, but I know that Sehic and I gave an order to our assistant commander for security and our assistant commander for morale to make a report to the brigade with regard to this matter, and I think that was done. Whether this was sent further on, this report, I mean, that is something I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. At this stage, what I'd like to do is show you some documents, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, if we could please bring document D744 on the screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Omerasevic, are you able to see that document clearly? It's the document on the left-hand side of your screen that I'd like you to look at. Are you able to read the writing?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED OMERASEVIC
utterances.text: Regular daily combat report. Sent. Situation and activities of the enemy -- the enemy, UN forces, and MO.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Would you -- could you confirm that what we see in front of us is a regular daily combat report dated the 11th of September, 1995 and it's going from the 328th Mountain Brigade. It has a confidential number, 02/2-1139/95, and it's going to the 35th Division.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED OMERASEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I -- what I see is that that is what the report says, but this is the first time I see this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I appreciate that this is a -- a document that you have never seen before, but if I could perhaps ask you to -- to take a look at some parts of it. Perhaps, first of all, if we could look at page 5 in the English and page 3 in the B/C/S version. If we can look at the bottom of the page in the B/C/S. We can see there that the document bears the name of Fuad Zilkic, who was the commander of the 328th Brigade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED OMERASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, if we could just look at the next page in both document, please, just to ascertain one matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And can you confirm, Mr. Omerasevic, that this page here, this document certifies that the report that we just looked at is a true copy of the original and was found in the archives of the ARBiH?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED OMERASEVIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as I can say. I mean, I can only make assumptions. I can't confirm that I perhaps sometime did have this -- the original in my hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I appreciate that. If we can return back to the first page of both documents, please. If we can scroll down the English version, please. Down to the bottom, please. It's right, isn't it, that we can see there a heading which says, number 2, "Situation and activities of brigade forces"? Do you see that heading?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED OMERASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And if we can go to the second page in the English version, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, what I'm interested in is -- is about one-third the way down the English screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Can you see there a subheading, Mr. Omerasevic, which says "Activities of the units"? It's about three-quarters of the way down the screen.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED OMERASEVIC
utterances.text: "Activities of the units"? Yes. Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And what we can see in here is Major Zilkic is given -- giving information about the battalions of the 328th Brigade, and he says here that "The 5th Battalion has designated forces of the strength of 1 mountain company for active b/d." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED OMERASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And does "b/d" mean combat operations?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED OMERASEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I assume that that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And it also goes on to say that the "Battalions are carrying out their regular tasks." Is that so?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED OMERASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So you'd agree with me that in this report, Major Zilkic is describing the situation relating to the battalions on the 11th of September and he's also included information about the 5th Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED OMERASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If I can carry on in the document. If we can turn to page 3 in the English and page 2 in the B/C/S version. And if we can scroll down the page in the English, please. Do you see there within section number 4, which is headed "Losses in personnel," there is some information about members of the ARBiH that have been slightly wounded?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED OMERASEVIC
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And within the part that deals with people that have been slightly wounded, we can see that there is information that relates to two members of the 5th Battalion of the 328th Brigade, Rasim Sogolj and Mihret Sogolj. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED OMERASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Did you know these two people by any chance?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED OMERASEVIC
utterances.text: I know Sogolj Mihret, but Rasim, not directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And as far as you were aware, is it right that Mihret Sogolj was -- was injured during the September operations?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED OMERASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, by a shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, the last thing on the document. If we could look at page 4, please. Your Honours, I -- I'd ask that this document be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is the document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 971.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, if we could please look at document D745.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Omerasevic, this is a one-page report. I appreciate that you've probably never seen this document before, but could you confirm for us that what we see on the screen in front of us is an interim operations report dated the 11th of September, 1995 from the 328th Mountain Brigade to the 35th Division.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter could not hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Could you just repeat that answer again, please. The interpreter didn't hear your answer.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED OMERASEVIC
utterances.text: I do see the report. That's what I said. I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And, again, can you confirm that this report bears the name of Fuad Zilkic at the -- at the bottom of it.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED OMERASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And can you confirm that in looking at the report, what we can see is that Major Zilkic has given information to the 35th Division about one of the -- one of his subordinate units, the 2nd Battalion?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED OMERASEVIC
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And we can see that the information that Major Zilkic is describing concerns events that took place about 1800 hours on the evening of the 11th of September. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED OMERASEVIC
utterances.text: Well, according to this, yes. However, this report which is on this page was far away from me at that point in time. It was on a completely different side, if I can put it that way. Say, 20 kilometres, as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to -- I've let it go on a bit, but I'm going to object to any further questions of this witness with regard to this document. It has nothing to do with anything the witness was -- it has nothing to do with the 5th Battalion. He's already said this was far away from him. And I think any further questions about this document is just going to be him reading the document and speculating.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask that I be given the chance, the opportunity to continue putting one or two foundational questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: There is an objection, sir. Deal with the objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm still asking foundational questions to this witness. It's my submission that the objection is -- it's too early, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm afraid, Mr. Robson, if you are not going to deal with the objection, then I'm going to rule you out of order in any further questions. Your colleague is saying no further questions because of what the witness told you. Now, you've got to deal with that; otherwise, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- I must support her objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I have asked one or two questions of this witness. I still have further questions to -- to put to this witness to ascertain what knowledge he -- he may have as to the content of this document, and I would ask for leave to continue to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Leave --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Leave is denied. The objection is upheld.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll put this document away. If it could be marked, please, for identification before I do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the document please be marked for identification and be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be MFI 972.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And if we could please bring up document D746 on the screens, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Omerasevic, this is similar to the first document that I showed you. Could you please confirm that what we can see in front of us is a regular daily combat report dated the 12th of September, 1995 from the 328th Mountain Brigade to the 35th Division.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED OMERASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, if we can turn to page 5 in the English and page 3 in the B/C/S version. If we could look at the bottom of the page in the B/C/S. Could you confirm that this document has come from Major Fuad Zilkic.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED OMERASEVIC
utterances.text: His name is signed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If we could please return back to the first page in both documents. If we can scroll down in -- in the English version, please. And also in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Like last time, can you see there a section which is headed, number 2, "Situation and activities of brigade forces"?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED OMERASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that, again, this section contains information about your unit, the 5th Battalion, and specifically it states: "526 fighters are manning the l/o in the z/o of the 4th, 5th, and the 1st Battalions"? Do you -- do you see that, Mr. Omerasevic? It is --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED OMERASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And staying with this section, if we can just turn over on to the English version, please. Before I do so, can you just confirm: What does "L/0" mean? Is it line of defence?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED OMERASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And z/o, does that mean zone of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED OMERASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And is it right that in this section, there is further information which says "The focus of activities is on conducting decisive defence in the l/o of the z/o of the 2nd and 3rd Battalions and taking control of the newly reached l/o with forces of the 3rd, 4th, 5th, and 1st Battalion of the 328th Brigade." That's in -- it's in the bottom third of the screen in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED OMERASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see that. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And beneath that, we can see it states -- it gives information about specific combat activities, and we can see here that place names are mentioned. We can see that -- that Cevaljusa is one of the names mentioned. And it also goes on to say that specific combat activities include: "Taking control of the aforementioned l/o, line of defence, has started at 0700 hours this morning with forces of the 3rd, 4th, 5th, and 1st Battalion." Does -- does this information that we see here correspond with what you were telling us earlier about what your units did on the 11th and 12th of September?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED OMERASEVIC
utterances.text: I think that this does correspond, but I don't know if I registered the dates of the statements properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd ask that this document be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 973.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Omerasevic. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Madam Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I have no questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Sartorio. Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have a question. Witness, in the reports that you saw on the basis of these documents that were shown to you by the Defence, in addition to combat activities, was there supposed to be a reference to the capturing of prisoners of war too?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED OMERASEVIC
utterances.text: I think there should have been, if people knew about them, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So why was that not done, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED OMERASEVIC
utterances.text: Well, whether the brigade commander knew about these prisoners or not is something I don't know. If he did know about this, it certainly should have been contained in the report, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] However, the subordinate units, were they duty-bound to report to the commander about that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED OMERASEVIC
utterances.text: They were duty-bound to do that, and I certainly said at the beginning that as far as I'm concerned and the battalion commander, the two assistant commanders for morale and security were instructed to inform the brigade command, and that was done. At that time, on the premises, I ordered the company commander to make a list of documents -- or rather, of the persons who were taken prisoner. But then this group of Arabs barged in and they prevented that, so I don't know whether at that moment Sogolj [Realtime transcript read in error "Sokolj"] managed to write down the names of all the persons. I don't know how many names he registered. And then he was supposed to make a report in terms of the hierarchy in the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you know nothing in relation to this report. You just know that there was an order that was issued by yourself and your superior officer.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED OMERASEVIC
utterances.text: And all the rest of the time I was out in the field, and I see that this report of the brigade corresponds to that, my movement from one area to another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Judge Harhoff? Madam Sartorio, any questions arising from the Judge's questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I think there needs to be a correction on the record, Your Honour, in terms of the person that he -- I think it's misspelled. And so we could ask the witness for the name of that person again, because it's been several pages and lines so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: The name at line 22 -- page 22.20. It says S-o-k-o-l-j. And I'm not -- it's not consistent with what is in the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Witness, can you tell us -- if you can look at the screen at page 22, line 20, sir. There's a name there called Sokolj. It's spelled S-o-k-o-l-j. Is that the correct spelling? First of all, is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it depends on the context. This very word, "Sokolj," in our language it doesn't really mean much. It can be "Sogolj," though.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's Note: S-o-g-o-l-j.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In -- in your statement, sir, how did you write this word?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't see the context in Bosnian. I don't know. It may be Sogolj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Sartorio, I think you'll have to either re-examine this witness and correct that. If you have got problems, I'm not able to help you, because I don't know the context. What do you plan to do, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I'll let it go, Your Honour. I have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any questions from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Omerasevic, you said that Sogolj managed to write down the names of the prisoners of war. Could you tell me, who was it, if anyone, who prepared a list that day?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED OMERASEVIC
utterances.text: I said that I told the company commander, Sogolj, at that point to make this list. I issued that task to him. But quickly another group of Arabs appeared, and that prevented him from doing it. So I don't know if he managed to start anything or to write down any names. I think this is what I said in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And do you know, was Mr. Karahasanovic there at all?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Does that arise from the Judge's questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, we've heard significant evidence in this case that a list was prepared by somebody on that day, and I'm just trying to clarify who the author of the list was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But that doesn't arise from the Judge's questions, does it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're leading new evidence now. The Prosecution is going to want to -- to re-examine on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, in this case, we've had -- the Trial Chamber has received evidence of a list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed. And -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And we've heard evidence today that suggests that that list may have been prepared by a man called Sogolj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: What I'm trying to ascertain is whether it's the same list or a different --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: -- list or something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But shouldn't you have asked about this other person -- what's his name again -- before -- this Karahasanovic, shouldn't you have asked about him in your cross-examination, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is something which has just arisen from Judge Lattanzi's question, this answer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: -- answer suggesting that Sogolj --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That was precisely my question to you, does this arise out of -- and you just wouldn't answer me. You've just told me that you've got evidence that this came from somebody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: It arises out of Judge Lattanzi's question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: No. I object, Your Honour. I don't -- I think if we go back to Judge Lattanzi's question, it has nothing to do with the list or Karahasanovic or anything of that sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to clarify something. Witness in responding to my question clearly said - and I refer to page where this is stated - that he does not know whether the list -- I would like to find the page in order to be able to quote exactly what the witness said. He said that he did not know whether the list was drafted because this action was interrupted. And Mr. Robson perhaps didn't precisely follow, and I think perhaps -- or I hope that this is what the matter is. And now he asked: You said that somebody drafted that list. But that is not true. The witness did not say that. The witness clearly said that he doesn't know anything about that. If you look at page 22, the question put by Mr. Robson on page 24, the -- that place is where the answer of the witness is recorded, and Mr. Robson cannot continue to put questions to the witness on the assumption that the witness really knew that the list was made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge. Anything further, Mr. Robson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I -- I take it, Your Honour, that -- that I'm not permitted to pursue this area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. No further questions, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Sir, that brings us to the end of your testimony. Thank you very much for coming to testify before the Trial Chamber. You are now excused. You may stand down. And please travel well back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: We have no further witnesses for this morning, Your Honour, as discussed on Friday, I believe, with Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll take a break and come back at quarter to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] The Trial Chamber now is going to give its ruling. I beg your pardon. The Trial Chamber is now going to give its ruling on two oral motions by the Prosecution that were made on Friday, the 7th of December, 2007. In the first motion, the Prosecution requested that the Chamber grant leave pursuant to Rule 50 of the Rules to withdraw count 3 of the indictment, which is rape, and violation of the laws or customs of war. The Defence agreed with the Prosecution's request. The Trial Chamber has considered the oral submissions by the parties and came to the conclusion that the withdrawal of a count after the accused has entered a plea and on which the Prosecution has led evidence would not be in the interests of justice because the accused could be tried again on that count. For these reasons, the motion is denied. In the second motion, the Prosecution requested that the Chamber reconsider its decision of the 5th December 2007 admitting into evidence the written statement of Witness DRW-1, pursuant to Rule 92 bis, subject to DRW-1 appearing for cross-examination. As DRW-1 would under no circumstances be available for cross-examination, the Prosecution asks that the evidence pertinent to count 3 be redacted from the statement, under which condition the Defence would renounce their -- the right to cross-examine her. The Trial Chamber takes the view that pursuant to Rule 92 ter, which is referred to by Rule 92 bis (C), the unavailability of DRW-1 for cross-examination results in her statement not being in evidence. The Chamber, however, decides to grant the second motion and allows the paragraph concerning count 3 to be redacted and admits the statement of DRW-1 in evidence pursuant to Rule 92 bis. Fine. Thank you very much. Those are the two motions that were outstanding. The one last thing -- well, not the very last, but last but one, maybe. We have the last motion by the Prosecution pursuant to Rule 92 bis for next year's witnesses. Because there may not be sufficient time when we come back to give a decision and to enable the Prosecution to schedule their witnesses, where the Chamber felt it must just find out from the Defence whether they has a position with respect to those motions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, in respect of the sixth motion, concerning two witnesses, Vukovic and Negovetic, the Defence's position is this: In respect of Mr. Vukovic, we do not oppose his statement being admitted into evidence without cross-examination. In respect of Mr. Negovetic, we will be inviting the Trial Chamber to rule that he should attend for cross-examination, and we will be filing our substantive response this morning, any moment now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Robson. Just before I say the last thing, do the parties have anything to raise, this being most probably the last day of the year that we are going to be together? Madam Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: The Prosecution has nothing, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Sartorio. Mr. Robson or Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence has nothing, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. In that event, then, as I've said, this is the last day of the year before -- that we are together. The Trial Chamber would like to just take this opportunity to wish everybody a pleasant restive season and hopefully we can come back in the new year refreshed and ready to move on with the job. Please have a merry Christmas and a splendid new year. Court adjourned to the 15th of January at 2.15 in courtroom II. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 15th day of January, 2008, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 10.52 a.m.,
